assessment.title: BeHistorical Era 2 Exam - Regional Worlds & Networks, c. 1200-1450 (AP Units 1-2) - Version 2.1

material.mattext:
Stimulus A — Song China, c. 1200–1450

A historian describes a state in which educated scholar-officials staffed an extensive imperial administration. At the same time, improved rice cultivation, canal transportation, paper money, expanding cities, and large-scale production of goods such as porcelain and textiles supported a highly commercialized economy. Confucian learning remained central to elite culture even as economic life changed.

Use this stimulus for Questions 1–4.

Question 1. Which institution most directly explains how the state described in the stimulus staffed its government?
A hereditary military aristocracy that held autonomous fiefs
A Confucian civil service system that recruited scholar-officials for an imperial bureaucracy
A network of merchant guilds that selected provincial governors
A decentralized vassal system in which nobles exchanged military service for land

Stimulus A — Song China, c. 1200–1450

A historian describes a state in which educated scholar-officials staffed an extensive imperial administration. At the same time, improved rice cultivation, canal transportation, paper money, expanding cities, and large-scale production of goods such as porcelain and textiles supported a highly commercialized economy. Confucian learning remained central to elite culture even as economic life changed.

Use this stimulus for Questions 1–4.

Question 2. Which development most directly contributed to the agricultural and urban growth described in the stimulus?
The spread of fast-ripening Champa rice together with improved internal transportation
The adoption of the camel saddle and expansion of desert caravan routes
The spread of the three-field system from western Europe into China
A shift from peasant farming to plantation slavery throughout the Song economy

Stimulus A — Song China, c. 1200–1450

A historian describes a state in which educated scholar-officials staffed an extensive imperial administration. At the same time, improved rice cultivation, canal transportation, paper money, expanding cities, and large-scale production of goods such as porcelain and textiles supported a highly commercialized economy. Confucian learning remained central to elite culture even as economic life changed.

Use this stimulus for Questions 1–4.

Question 3. Which evidence from the period best illustrates the cultural continuity described in the stimulus?
The spread of Sufi devotional orders across the Islamic world
The growing political authority of Christian monasteries in western Europe
The influence of Neo-Confucian ideas on education, family hierarchy, and government
The replacement of Confucian learning by Buddhism in Song state institutions

Stimulus A — Song China, c. 1200–1450

A historian describes a state in which educated scholar-officials staffed an extensive imperial administration. At the same time, improved rice cultivation, canal transportation, paper money, expanding cities, and large-scale production of goods such as porcelain and textiles supported a highly commercialized economy. Confucian learning remained central to elite culture even as economic life changed.

Use this stimulus for Questions 1–4.

Question 4. Which comparison between Song China and western Europe during the same period is most accurate?
Both relied primarily on hereditary warrior elites to staff centralized bureaucracies
Song China maintained a more centralized bureaucratic state, while much of western Europe remained politically fragmented
Western Europe used civil service examinations more extensively than Song China
Both regions eliminated local elites by placing merchants directly in charge of government

Stimulus B — Dar al-Islam after Abbasid fragmentation

By the thirteenth century, Abbasid political authority had weakened and new Islamic states ruled much of Southwest Asia, Egypt, Anatolia, and South Asia. Turkic military elites became important in several of these states. Yet merchants, scholars, Sufi teachers, pilgrims, and legal traditions continued to connect communities across a broad Islamic world. Centers such as Cairo, Delhi, and Tabriz supported scholarship even after Baghdad was sacked in 1258.

Use this stimulus for Questions 5–8.

Question 5. Which development best explains the rise of new Islamic political entities described in the stimulus?
The decline of Abbasid political authority allowed regional rulers and Turkic military elites to establish new states
The Crusades permanently removed Muslim rulers from Southwest Asia
Merchant diasporas replaced states as the main form of political organization
The conversion of most Islamic rulers to Christianity fractured the caliphate

Stimulus B — Dar al-Islam after Abbasid fragmentation

By the thirteenth century, Abbasid political authority had weakened and new Islamic states ruled much of Southwest Asia, Egypt, Anatolia, and South Asia. Turkic military elites became important in several of these states. Yet merchants, scholars, Sufi teachers, pilgrims, and legal traditions continued to connect communities across a broad Islamic world. Centers such as Cairo, Delhi, and Tabriz supported scholarship even after Baghdad was sacked in 1258.

Use this stimulus for Questions 5–8.

Question 6. Which historical pattern is best demonstrated by the stimulus?
Political fragmentation necessarily caused the disappearance of shared religious traditions
Islamic culture remained geographically confined to areas directly ruled from Baghdad
Political decentralization could coexist with continuing religious, commercial, and intellectual networks
New Islamic states ended long-distance trade in order to strengthen local economies

Stimulus B — Dar al-Islam after Abbasid fragmentation

By the thirteenth century, Abbasid political authority had weakened and new Islamic states ruled much of Southwest Asia, Egypt, Anatolia, and South Asia. Turkic military elites became important in several of these states. Yet merchants, scholars, Sufi teachers, pilgrims, and legal traditions continued to connect communities across a broad Islamic world. Centers such as Cairo, Delhi, and Tabriz supported scholarship even after Baghdad was sacked in 1258.

Use this stimulus for Questions 5–8.

Question 7. Which additional evidence would best support the claim that Islam continued to spread through networks even when no single caliphate controlled the Islamic world?
Sufi teachers and Muslim merchants established communities along African and Asian trade routes
Mamluk forces defeated a Mongol army at Ain Jalut
The Delhi Sultanate collected taxes from agricultural communities in northern India
The Abbasid caliph continued to claim religious prestige before 1258

Stimulus B — Dar al-Islam after Abbasid fragmentation

By the thirteenth century, Abbasid political authority had weakened and new Islamic states ruled much of Southwest Asia, Egypt, Anatolia, and South Asia. Turkic military elites became important in several of these states. Yet merchants, scholars, Sufi teachers, pilgrims, and legal traditions continued to connect communities across a broad Islamic world. Centers such as Cairo, Delhi, and Tabriz supported scholarship even after Baghdad was sacked in 1258.

Use this stimulus for Questions 5–8.

Question 8. Which broader effect most directly resulted from the intellectual interactions described in the stimulus?
Scholars increasingly rejected mathematics and astronomy as foreign traditions
Knowledge in medicine, mathematics, philosophy, and geography circulated across regional and cultural boundaries
The destruction of Baghdad ended major centers of Islamic scholarship everywhere
European scholars became less connected to Greek and Islamic intellectual traditions

Stimulus C — Two state-building systems

Evidence A: A large Andean state connected distant provinces with roads and relay stations. Officials used record-keeping systems, while communities supplied labor for agriculture, construction, military service, and state storehouses.

Evidence B: A southeastern African state accumulated wealth from cattle, regional resources, and commerce linking the interior to Indian Ocean ports. Monumental dry-stone architecture displayed elite power.

Use this stimulus for Questions 9–12.

Question 9. Which state is represented by Evidence A?
The Mexica Empire
The Inca Empire
The Maya city-states
Cahokia

Stimulus C — Two state-building systems

Evidence A: A large Andean state connected distant provinces with roads and relay stations. Officials used record-keeping systems, while communities supplied labor for agriculture, construction, military service, and state storehouses.

Evidence B: A southeastern African state accumulated wealth from cattle, regional resources, and commerce linking the interior to Indian Ocean ports. Monumental dry-stone architecture displayed elite power.

Use this stimulus for Questions 9–12.

Question 10. Which comparison between Evidence A and Evidence B is most historically defensible?
Both states relied on identical systems of coerced agricultural labor
Both states used access to resources to strengthen political authority, although they mobilized those resources in different ways
Both states depended primarily on trans-Saharan trade for political revenue
Both states organized their governments around Confucian examination systems

Stimulus C — Two state-building systems

Evidence A: A large Andean state connected distant provinces with roads and relay stations. Officials used record-keeping systems, while communities supplied labor for agriculture, construction, military service, and state storehouses.

Evidence B: A southeastern African state accumulated wealth from cattle, regional resources, and commerce linking the interior to Indian Ocean ports. Monumental dry-stone architecture displayed elite power.

Use this stimulus for Questions 9–12.

Question 11. Which combination of institutions most directly helped the state in Evidence A administer a large and geographically difficult territory?
Chinampa agriculture and merchant guilds
Road networks, labor obligations, state storehouses, and record keeping
Caravanserai, camel saddles, and bills of exchange
Feudal vassalage, serfdom, and Church courts

Stimulus C — Two state-building systems

Evidence A: A large Andean state connected distant provinces with roads and relay stations. Officials used record-keeping systems, while communities supplied labor for agriculture, construction, military service, and state storehouses.

Evidence B: A southeastern African state accumulated wealth from cattle, regional resources, and commerce linking the interior to Indian Ocean ports. Monumental dry-stone architecture displayed elite power.

Use this stimulus for Questions 9–12.

Question 12. Evidence B best supports which claim about African state building from c. 1200 to c. 1450?
African states generally developed in isolation from long-distance commerce
Participation in regional and Indian Ocean commerce could provide wealth that rulers used to reinforce state power
Christianity was the principal source of legitimacy for all major African states
Most African states depended on centralized civil service examinations

Stimulus D — Silk Roads commerce

A merchant crossing Central Asia travels in a caravan and stops at fortified roadside inns where animals can rest and goods can be protected. Rather than carry all of his wealth in coins, he uses credit and written financial arrangements. Cities located where major routes intersect attract merchants, translators, artisans, and religious travelers.

Use this stimulus for Questions 13–16.

Question 13. Which institution described in the stimulus most directly reduced the logistical difficulties of overland trade?
Caravanserai that provided secure lodging, supplies, and space for pack animals
State storehouses that collected mit'a labor payments
Maritime ports timed to monsoon wind cycles
Feudal manors that tied serfs to agricultural estates

Stimulus D — Silk Roads commerce

A merchant crossing Central Asia travels in a caravan and stops at fortified roadside inns where animals can rest and goods can be protected. Rather than carry all of his wealth in coins, he uses credit and written financial arrangements. Cities located where major routes intersect attract merchants, translators, artisans, and religious travelers.

Use this stimulus for Questions 13–16.

Question 14. Why were credit arrangements and bills of exchange historically significant to Silk Roads commerce?
They eliminated the need for any currency in long-distance trade
They reduced some risks and costs associated with transporting large amounts of coin or precious metal
They placed all private trade under direct control of imperial governments
They made overland transportation less expensive than maritime shipping for bulk goods

Stimulus D — Silk Roads commerce

A merchant crossing Central Asia travels in a caravan and stops at fortified roadside inns where animals can rest and goods can be protected. Rather than carry all of his wealth in coins, he uses credit and written financial arrangements. Cities located where major routes intersect attract merchants, translators, artisans, and religious travelers.

Use this stimulus for Questions 13–16.

Question 15. Which pair of cities best illustrates the urban pattern described in the stimulus?
Calicut and Kilwa
Timbuktu and Gao
Kashgar and Samarkand
Cuzco and Tenochtitlan

Stimulus D — Silk Roads commerce

A merchant crossing Central Asia travels in a caravan and stops at fortified roadside inns where animals can rest and goods can be protected. Rather than carry all of his wealth in coins, he uses credit and written financial arrangements. Cities located where major routes intersect attract merchants, translators, artisans, and religious travelers.

Use this stimulus for Questions 13–16.

Question 16. Why did luxury goods such as silk and porcelain figure prominently in long-distance overland trade?
Their high value relative to their weight could justify costly overland transportation
Governments prohibited merchants from carrying food or other ordinary goods
Luxury goods were produced only in Central Asian trading cities
Merchants on the Silk Roads had no access to maritime trade routes

Stimulus E — The Mongol Empire and Eurasian exchange

The map shows Mongol-controlled territory and major routes extending across much of Eurasia. After the empire divided into khanates, Mongol rulers continued to protect many merchants, maintain relay stations, and move officials and specialists across long distances.

Use this stimulus for Questions 17–20.

Question 17. Which development most directly increased the movement of merchants and travelers across much of the territory shown on the map?
Mongol protection of major routes and efforts to punish attacks on authorized travelers
The permanent abolition of warfare among all Eurasian states
The replacement of overland exchange with a single maritime trade system
The political unification of Eurasia under one Mongol government until 1450

Stimulus E — The Mongol Empire and Eurasian exchange

The map shows Mongol-controlled territory and major routes extending across much of Eurasia. After the empire divided into khanates, Mongol rulers continued to protect many merchants, maintain relay stations, and move officials and specialists across long distances.

Use this stimulus for Questions 17–20.

Question 18. Which Mongol institution most directly helped rulers communicate across the long distances shown on the map?
The Yam relay system of stations and fresh horses
Caravanserai financed by private merchant associations
Bills of exchange issued by urban banking families
The mit'a system of rotational labor service

Stimulus E — The Mongol Empire and Eurasian exchange

The map shows Mongol-controlled territory and major routes extending across much of Eurasia. After the empire divided into khanates, Mongol rulers continued to protect many merchants, maintain relay stations, and move officials and specialists across long distances.

Use this stimulus for Questions 17–20.

Question 19. Which development was an unintended consequence of the greater Eurasian connectivity associated with Mongol rule?
The rapid transmission of epidemic disease along commercial and travel routes
The disappearance of long-distance merchant communities from Central Asia
The end of cultural and technological transfers between China and western Eurasia
The permanent decline of cities located along major caravan routes

Stimulus E — The Mongol Empire and Eurasian exchange

The map shows Mongol-controlled territory and major routes extending across much of Eurasia. After the empire divided into khanates, Mongol rulers continued to protect many merchants, maintain relay stations, and move officials and specialists across long distances.

Use this stimulus for Questions 17–20.

Question 20. Which statement best describes continuity and change in Eurasian exchange under the Mongols?
The Mongols created trans-Eurasian trade routes where none had previously existed
Existing exchange networks intensified because new political conditions reduced some barriers to movement
The Mongols ended overland trade and redirected commerce entirely to the Indian Ocean
The Mongol khanates abolished local cultural practices in order to standardize trade

Stimulus F — Indian Ocean port city

A traveler reaches a major Indian Ocean port and finds merchants from Arabia, Persia, India, East Africa, and Southeast Asia living in distinct neighborhoods. Ships arrive and depart according to seasonal wind patterns. Mosques, temples, warehouses, and markets stand near one another, and merchants sometimes remain for months before winds permit the return voyage.

Use this stimulus for Questions 21–24.

Question 21. Which environmental factor most directly explains why merchants in the stimulus sometimes remained in port for months?
Seasonal monsoon wind patterns
Winter freezing of Central Asian mountain passes
Annual flooding of the Niger River
Irregular rainfall across the Sahara

Stimulus F — Indian Ocean port city

A traveler reaches a major Indian Ocean port and finds merchants from Arabia, Persia, India, East Africa, and Southeast Asia living in distinct neighborhoods. Ships arrive and depart according to seasonal wind patterns. Mosques, temples, warehouses, and markets stand near one another, and merchants sometimes remain for months before winds permit the return voyage.

Use this stimulus for Questions 21–24.

Question 22. The merchant neighborhoods described in the stimulus most directly contributed to which development?
The complete replacement of local cultures by foreign merchant traditions
The creation of diasporic communities in which imported and local traditions interacted
The political unification of the entire Indian Ocean basin under one empire
The decline of port cities as merchants avoided permanent settlements abroad

Stimulus F — Indian Ocean port city

A traveler reaches a major Indian Ocean port and finds merchants from Arabia, Persia, India, East Africa, and Southeast Asia living in distinct neighborhoods. Ships arrive and depart according to seasonal wind patterns. Mosques, temples, warehouses, and markets stand near one another, and merchants sometimes remain for months before winds permit the return voyage.

Use this stimulus for Questions 21–24.

Question 23. Which technological combination most directly supported the maritime commerce described in the stimulus?
Camel saddles and caravanserai
Stirrups and composite bows
Lateen sails, improved ship designs, and navigational tools such as the compass or astrolabe
Civil service examinations and paper money

Stimulus F — Indian Ocean port city

A traveler reaches a major Indian Ocean port and finds merchants from Arabia, Persia, India, East Africa, and Southeast Asia living in distinct neighborhoods. Ships arrive and depart according to seasonal wind patterns. Mosques, temples, warehouses, and markets stand near one another, and merchants sometimes remain for months before winds permit the return voyage.

Use this stimulus for Questions 21–24.

Question 24. Which broader conclusion is best supported by the stimulus?
Knowledge of environmental patterns combined with maritime technology enabled extensive long-distance commercial networks
Indian Ocean commerce expanded only when Mongol rulers directly controlled port cities
Maritime trade depended on eliminating cultural differences among merchants
Environmental conditions made sustained long-distance sea trade less reliable than local exchange

Stimulus G — Mali and trans-Saharan exchange

A fourteenth-century West African ruler controls territory connected to major gold-producing regions and taxes commerce moving across the Sahara. During his pilgrimage to Mecca, his wealth draws attention throughout the Islamic world. Cities in his empire grow as centers of trade, Islamic learning, and manuscript culture.

Use this stimulus for Questions 25–28.

Question 25. Which economic factor most directly explains the ruler's wealth and the growth of the state described in the stimulus?
Control of and taxation on gold and other goods moving through trans-Saharan trade
Profits from Chinese porcelain factories owned by the West African state
Direct control of Indian Ocean shipping between India and Southeast Asia
Agricultural tribute collected through the Andean mit'a system

Stimulus G — Mali and trans-Saharan exchange

A fourteenth-century West African ruler controls territory connected to major gold-producing regions and taxes commerce moving across the Sahara. During his pilgrimage to Mecca, his wealth draws attention throughout the Islamic world. Cities in his empire grow as centers of trade, Islamic learning, and manuscript culture.

Use this stimulus for Questions 25–28.

Question 26. Which transportation technology was most important to the expansion of the commerce described in the stimulus?
The lateen sail
The camel saddle
The stirrup used by steppe cavalry
The Grand Canal

Stimulus G — Mali and trans-Saharan exchange

A fourteenth-century West African ruler controls territory connected to major gold-producing regions and taxes commerce moving across the Sahara. During his pilgrimage to Mecca, his wealth draws attention throughout the Islamic world. Cities in his empire grow as centers of trade, Islamic learning, and manuscript culture.

Use this stimulus for Questions 25–28.

Question 27. Which argument is best supported by the stimulus?
Long-distance commerce could increase both state revenue and a ruler's visibility beyond his own region
Islamic connections generally weakened the authority of West African rulers
African states were economically separate from broader Afro-Eurasian exchange
Trade wealth mattered to merchants but had little relationship to political power

Stimulus G — Mali and trans-Saharan exchange

A fourteenth-century West African ruler controls territory connected to major gold-producing regions and taxes commerce moving across the Sahara. During his pilgrimage to Mecca, his wealth draws attention throughout the Islamic world. Cities in his empire grow as centers of trade, Islamic learning, and manuscript culture.

Use this stimulus for Questions 25–28.

Question 28. Which additional development most directly resulted from the connections described in the stimulus?
The growth of Islamic scholarship and manuscript culture in cities such as Timbuktu
The spread of Neo-Confucian civil service examinations across West Africa
The creation of European feudal manors along caravan routes
The widespread conversion of West African rulers to Buddhism
Question 29. Which comparison best explains how belief systems could reinforce political and social authority in Song China and medieval western Europe?
Song and European rulers both relied mainly on Islamic legal scholars whose religious authority controlled appointments to major state offices.
Song rulers drew on Confucian ideals and scholar-official institutions, while European rulers drew on Christianity and Church institutions.
Song and European rulers both separated religious and ethical traditions from education, law, social hierarchy, and political legitimacy.
European rulers relied on Confucian examination systems, while Song emperors relied on bishops and monasteries to staff the bureaucracy.
Question 30. Which development best illustrates the influence of Chinese cultural traditions on neighboring East Asian societies?
Korean elites adopted Islamic law and Arabic script through sustained participation in trans-Saharan commercial and scholarly networks.
Japanese elites adopted Hindu temple patronage and caste institutions through regular contact with merchants from maritime South Asia.
Vietnamese rulers organized government through feudal vassalage modeled directly on the political institutions of western European kingdoms.
Korean elites adopted Confucian educational and bureaucratic traditions while adapting those traditions to local political institutions.
Question 31. Which comparison between the Mexica and Inca empires is most accurate?
Both extracted resources from subject peoples, but the Mexica emphasized tribute while the Inca organized extensive state labor obligations.
Both governed through examination-trained bureaucrats, but Mexica officials studied Confucian classics while Inca officials studied Buddhist texts.
Both depended on maritime merchant diasporas, but the Mexica taxed Indian Ocean ports while the Inca controlled Swahili coastal commerce.
Both were loose alliances of independent city-states, and neither developed systems for tribute, labor taxation, or imperial administration.
Question 32. Which evidence best explains how Ethiopian rulers strengthened political legitimacy during this period?
By recruiting government officials through Confucian examinations that tied political service to mastery of classical Chinese texts.
By controlling Mongol relay stations that connected Ethiopian rulers directly to the major overland trade routes of Eurasia.
By linking royal authority to an established Christian tradition and sacred claims about the legitimacy of the ruling dynasty.
By transferring political authority to merchant guilds that governed cities independently of kings and religious institutions.
Question 33. Which development most directly contributed to political decentralization in much of medieval western Europe?
Royal civil service examinations concentrated political authority in officials appointed through a centralized imperial bureaucracy.
Feudal ties dispersed military and political authority among kings, nobles, vassals, and other powerful local landholders.
Merchant councils gradually replaced kings and nobles, concentrating military authority in commercially powerful European cities.
Mongol governors standardized taxation and law across western Europe, reducing the independent political power of local nobles.
Question 34. Which comparison between state organization in Song China and western Europe is strongest?
Both regions organized government primarily through hereditary vassalage, with nobles holding autonomous lands in exchange for military service.
Western Europe relied more heavily on examination-trained administrators, while Song China delegated government to hereditary landholding nobles.
Both regions weakened landed elites by placing most political authority in urban merchant corporations and long-distance trading guilds.
Song China maintained a more centralized imperial bureaucracy, while western European authority remained more fragmented among local elites.
Question 35. Which evidence most directly demonstrates the commercialization of the Song economy?
Paper money, expanding urban markets, specialized manufacturing, and increasing internal and overseas commercial exchange.
Greater reliance on landed estates, reduced urban exchange, and a return to local barter and subsistence agricultural production.
Expansion of pastoral nomadism, declining canal traffic, and reduced production of porcelain and textiles for commercial markets.
Wider use of camel caravans, contraction of coastal commerce, and replacement of paper money with payments made mainly in livestock.
Question 36. The Bhakti movement in South Asia and Sufi traditions in the Islamic world are most useful for illustrating which broader process?
State governments increasingly limited religion to court rituals and prevented teachers from forming popular devotional communities.
Popular devotional movements generally rejected both Islamic and Hindu traditions and created entirely separate religious systems.
Devotional movements could widen religious participation through personal piety, teachers, poetry, and locally adapted practices.
Religious participation became more restricted to hereditary elites as devotional teachers discouraged ordinary people from worship.
Question 37. Which statement best explains how rulers in South and Southeast Asia used religion to build or legitimize states?
The Delhi Sultanate and Vijayanagara rulers both eliminated religious diversity by imposing one uniform state faith on all communities.
Rulers patronized temples, monasteries, and sacred traditions to connect political authority with beliefs recognized by their subjects.
Khmer rulers avoided monumental religious building and separated temple institutions from taxation, labor, and royal legitimacy.
Majapahit and other maritime states strengthened authority by excluding foreign merchants and rejecting religious influences carried by trade.
Question 38. Which statement best explains the role of Christianity in medieval western European society?
Christian institutions created a centralized imperial bureaucracy in which clergy were selected through examinations and governed royal provinces.
Church leaders dismantled feudal relationships by transferring noble estates to peasants and prohibiting land-based military obligations.
Christian institutions remained largely separate from political life because kings prohibited clergy and monasteries from holding social influence.
Church institutions linked communities across fragmented territories and shaped education, social norms, law, and ideas of legitimate authority.
Question 39. Which factor was common to the expansion of the Silk Roads, Indian Ocean, and trans-Saharan networks from c. 1200 to c. 1450?
Transportation technologies and commercial practices adapted to each route made long-distance exchange more reliable and profitable.
Mongol states directly governed all three networks and imposed one legal and commercial system from Africa to the Indian Ocean.
Seasonal monsoon winds determined travel schedules on all three networks and made caravan movement predictable across deserts and steppes.
Camel caravans served as the main transportation system on all three networks and allowed merchants to move luxury and bulk goods.
Question 40. Which comparison between trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean commerce is most accurate?
Both depended on Mongol relay stations and imperial passports to protect merchants moving between major commercial cities.
Both transported most goods on large ocean-going ships that could move bulk cargo more efficiently than overland caravans.
Both relied on specialized knowledge and technologies adapted to demanding environmental conditions along their trade routes.
Both discouraged permanent trading cities because merchants generally traveled continuously rather than settling in commercial communities.
Question 41. Which development best illustrates how Indian Ocean commerce contributed to state formation?
Western European lords gained political authority by using monsoon navigation to expand agricultural estates and strengthen serfdom.
Swahili city-states gained wealth and political influence by linking East African interior resources to Indian Ocean commerce.
Mongol khanates expanded political control by taxing East African coastal ports and stationing cavalry along Indian Ocean sea lanes.
Inca rulers strengthened imperial administration by inviting Indian Ocean merchant diasporas to manage Andean roads and state storehouses.
Question 42. Which development best illustrates cultural syncretism produced by expanding networks of exchange?
Mongol rulers created cultural unity by requiring conquered peoples to abandon local religions and adopt one official Mongol belief system.
Western European peasants adopted the Inca mit'a labor system after trans-Saharan merchants introduced Andean political institutions.
Song officials replaced Confucian traditions with Christianity after foreign merchants gained control of education and bureaucratic appointments.
Swahili culture blended Bantu language and social traditions with Islamic and commercial influences carried through Indian Ocean exchange.
Question 43. Which development best demonstrates technological diffusion through expanding Afro-Eurasian networks?
Gunpowder technologies moved westward from China through Afro-Eurasian exchange and were adapted by societies in the Islamic world and Europe.
The Mexica tribute system moved eastward through Indian Ocean commerce and became a standard method of taxation in Song China.
European feudal institutions spread across Central Asia through Mongol conquest and replaced khanate-style imperial administration.
The Inca quipu spread through Silk Road merchants and became a common financial record-keeping technology in Eurasian cities.
Question 44. Which pair of developments best illustrates biological and environmental diffusion associated with increased connectivity?
The spread of civil service examinations into new empires and the adoption of feudal contracts by long-distance merchants.
The construction of monumental temples in new capitals and the increased collection of tribute from conquered populations.
The movement of new crop varieties into unfamiliar regions and the spread of epidemic pathogens along expanding trade routes.
The wider use of bills of exchange by merchants and the growth of credit arrangements in major commercial cities.
Question 45. Which causal sequence best explains the spread and demographic impact of the Black Death in the fourteenth century?
Political decentralization → collapse of long-distance commerce → growing isolation of major cities → faster transmission of epidemic disease.
Intensified interregional exchange → movement of disease vectors and pathogens → epidemic transmission → severe population decline.
Agricultural innovation → rapid population decline → lower urban density and reduced trade → greater vulnerability to plague across Eurasia.
Religious diffusion → disappearance of merchant communities → sustained population growth → widespread transmission of epidemic pathogens.
Question 46. In medieval western Europe, which relationship most directly connected agricultural production to local social and political hierarchy?
Scholar-officials received farmland after passing civil service examinations and entering centralized royal bureaucracies.
Merchant diasporas assigned compulsory rotational labor to rural communities through a European version of the mit'a system.
Pastoral clans supplied mounted warriors to local lords in exchange for caravanserai control and access to regional trade.
Serfs and peasants worked manorial lands and owed rents, labor services, or other customary dues to local lords.
Question 47. Which comparison between Silk Roads and Indian Ocean commerce is most accurate?
Both enabled economic and cultural exchange, but maritime shipping generally moved bulk goods more efficiently than overland caravans.
Both supported major commercial cities, but only Silk Road cities attracted permanent diasporic communities of foreign merchants and artisans.
Both depended on pack-animal caravans, but Indian Ocean merchants used camels mainly to transport cargo between distant island ports.
Both transmitted religious ideas, but only the Silk Roads carried technologies and scientific knowledge across regional boundaries.
Question 48. Which factor best explains the rise of powerful maritime states in Southeast Asia, including Majapahit and other states positioned near major sea routes?
Steppe cavalry gave island rulers control of overland routes and allowed them to tax Silk Road caravans crossing Central Asia.
Confucian examination systems supplied maritime rulers with revenue, reducing their need to tax merchants or control commercial ports.
Control of strategic ports and sea lanes allowed rulers to tax merchants, protect shipping, and profit directly from Indian Ocean commerce.
Excluding foreign merchants protected maritime rulers from outside cultural influence and produced greater wealth through political isolation.
Question 49. Which comparison between Mali and Great Zimbabwe best demonstrates the diversity of African state building?
Both gained wealth from long-distance trade, but Mali relied on Indian Ocean ports while Great Zimbabwe controlled the main trans-Saharan caravan routes.
Both gained wealth from long-distance trade, but Mali was tied to trans-Saharan gold commerce while Great Zimbabwe linked interior resources to Indian Ocean routes.
Both used long-distance commerce to expand, but Mali relied on Christian monastic networks while Great Zimbabwe built authority through Islamic law schools.
Both expanded through trade and taxation, but Mali recruited officials through Confucian examinations while Great Zimbabwe used Song-style provincial bureaucracy.
Question 50. Which thesis best compares the major Afro-Eurasian exchange networks from c. 1200 to c. 1450?
All three expanded because Mongol rule standardized laws, currencies, and transportation from the Sahara to the Indian Ocean, making regional geography much less important.
All three declined after 1200 because states restricted merchants and cultural exchange, although some protected cities maintained limited regional trade until 1450.
All three expanded mainly because predictable monsoon winds lowered travel costs across deserts, seas, and steppes, giving merchants a shared environmental advantage.
All three expanded through improved transport, commercial practices, and state support, but geography shaped travel methods, traded goods, and patterns of interaction.
